chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was in the women's tawaf (circumambulation) when the call for prayer was made. He said, 'He prays' (meaning the obligatory prayer). When he finishes, he completes (the remaining rounds) from where he stopped. And whoever is in tawaf and fears missing the Witr prayer, he stops the tawaf, prays Witr, and then completes his tawaf from where he left off. The reasoning in this is that this voluntary prayer is tied to a specific time; when its time passes, it is considered fulfilled. But tawaf is not like that, because it does not have a fixed time; if one delays it beyond its time, it is missed. This is indicated by what has been narrated:

key_terms.بَنَى: Bana (to build upon/complete from where one left off)

ai.seo_question: What should a person do if they are performing tawaf and the call to prayer is made?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential hierarchy between the time-bound nature of voluntary prayers (like Witr) and the continuous, non-time-bound status of Tawaf. It establishes that while obligatory prayers demand immediate cessation of ritual acts, voluntary prayers allow for a temporary pause where the worshipper can resume Tawaf from the exact point of interruption, preserving the integrity of the circumambulation.
